query: For a multi-phase eutectic high-entropy alloy exposed to simultaneous wear and corrosion at elevated temperature, what single mechanistic hypothesis could explain the accelerated coupled degradation and why it occurs? Specify a controlled comparison capable of distinguishing the proposed explanation, predict the changes in total degradation and the individual wear and corrosion responses relative to a matched baseline, define the relevant boundary conditions, identify supporting evidence, and give a clear falsification criterion.

generation.hypothesis: Accelerated degradation in the multi‐phase eutectic high‐entropy alloy arises from a synergistic wear–corrosion mechanism that is localized at the eutectic interphase boundaries. In these regions, mechanical wear at elevated temperatures preferentially removes or disrupts the protective oxide films on one phase (typically the more anodic, Al–Ni–rich phase) exposing it to corrosive attack, while the dissimilar, more cathodic phase remains comparatively inert. This creates galvanic micro-cells that intensify localized corrosion. The resulting corrosion damage further weakens the material at interphase regions, reducing its load-bearing capacity and accelerating wear, thereby establishing a positive feedback loop between the two degradation modes.
generation.material_initial_state: A multi-phase eutectic high‐entropy alloy with a fine, alternating lamellar microstructure (e.g., soft fcc and hard B2 phases) that, under static conditions, forms a uniform, protective oxide layer on its surfaces.
generation.intervention: Simultaneous exposure to sliding wear and corrosive environment at elevated temperatures that mechanically abrades the protective oxide film and promotes galvanic corrosion at the phase boundaries.
generation.conditions: Elevated temperature testing under a corrosive medium combined with cyclic sliding wear to induce both mechanical damage and chemical attack.
generation.structural_mediator: The eutectic lamellar interfaces between the dissimilar phases act as sites for galvanic coupling; mechanical wear preferentially exposes these interfaces by removing the protective oxide, thereby mediating the coupled degradation.
generation.mechanism: Mechanical wear at elevated temperature continuously disrupts and removes the protective oxide films at the interphase boundaries of the alternating lamellae. Once exposed, the anodic regions become preferentially attacked in a corrosive environment while the adjacent cathodic regions remain less affected. The resulting localized corrosion at these interfaces exacerbates microstructural degradation, which in turn lowers the resistance to further mechanical wear. This feedback loop between oxide removal, galvanic attack, and wear synergistically accelerates the overall degradation rate via the severe lattice distortion that characterizes multi-principal-element effects.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to a baseline condition (either alloys subjected to isolated wear or corrosion or alloys with a homogenized microstructure), the eutectic HEA under simultaneous wear–corrosion at high temperature will exhibit a greater total degradation. Specifically, one would observe an increase in overall wear rate and more pronounced localized pits or corrosion features at the phase interfaces, indicating that both wear and corrosion are enhanced compared to the baseline.
generation.baseline: A comparative case using either (a) testing the same alloy under isolated wear or isolated corrosion conditions at matching temperatures or (b) a homogenized version of the alloy (with minimized distinct phase boundaries) that reduces galvanic interactions.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis is expected to hold under high-temperature conditions (600–900 °C) in corrosive environments; its validity under room-temperature or non-corrosive conditions is not assumed.
generation.uncertainty: While the feedback between mechanical wear and localized corrosion at the interphase boundaries is expected to accelerate degradation, the quantitative contributions of each effect and the precise roles of the individual phases require further experimental investigation.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples: one with the as-cast, fine lamellar eutectic microstructure and another that has been homogenized via appropriate heat treatment to reduce the distinct interphase boundaries (and therefore minimize galvanic coupling). Subject both sets to identical simultaneous sliding wear and corrosion testing at an elevated temperature (e.g., 800 °C) in a corrosive medium.
measurements: Localized corrosion metrics (pit density and depth via SEM/EDS)
Integrity and composition of surface oxide layers (via XRD and XPS)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the homogenized samples (with reduced or absent distinct interphase boundaries) exhibit degradation rates (both wear and corrosion) similar to or greater than those of the as-cast eutectic samples, or if the as-cast samples do not show preferential corrosion at the phase boundaries despite comparable wear, then the hypothesized mechanism—that the coupling of localized wear-induced oxide removal and galvanic corrosion at eutectic interfaces accelerates degradation—would be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: High-entropy alloys (HEAs) can have either high strength or high ductility, and a simultaneous achievement of both still constitutes a tough challenge. The inferior castability and compositional segregation of HEAs are also obstacles for their technological applications. To tackle these problems, here we proposed a novel strategy to design HEAs using the eutectic alloy concept, i.e. to achieve a microstructure composed of alternating soft fcc and hard bcc phases. As a manifestation of this concept, an AlCoCrFeNi2.1 (atomic portion) eutectic high-entropy alloy (EHEA) was designed. The as-cast EHEA possessed a fine lamellar fcc/B2 microstructure, and showed an unprecedented combination of high tensile ductility and high fracture strength at room temperature. The excellent mechanical properties could be kept up to 700°C. This new alloy design strategy can be readily adapted to large-scale industrial production of HEAs with simultaneous high fracture strength and high ductility.

AbstractIn this study, the wear behaviour of a powder metallurgically produced AlCoCrFeNiTi0.5 high-entropy alloy (HEAs) is investigated at elevated temperatures. Spark plasma sintering (SPS) of inert gas atomised feedstock enables the production of dense bulk material. The microstructure evolution and phase formation are analysed. The high cooling rate in the atomisation process results in spherical powder with a microstructure comprising two finely distributed body-centred cubic phases. An additional phase with a complex crystal structure precipitates during SPS processing, while no coarsening of microstructural features occurs. The wear resistance under reciprocating wear conditions increases at elevated temperatures due to the formation of a protective oxide layer under atmospherical conditions. Additionally, the coefficient of friction (COF) slightly decreases with increasing temperature. SPS processing is suitable for the production of HEA bulk material.
